keywords: Hariphunchai National Museum, Lamphun museum, Phra Rod Lamphun, Hariphunchai artifacts, things to do in Lamphun
h1:
Hariphunchai National Museum
An Old City Told Through Real Relics
intro: Lamphun is one of the oldest towns in northern Thailand, going back more than 1,300 years to the Hariphunchai kingdom of Queen Chamadevi. If you want to understand what this town has been through, the Hariphunchai National Museum is the best place to start, because it gathers more than 2,000 genuine Buddha images, amulets, and inscriptions dug up around town. It sits right across from Wat Phra That Hariphunchai, so you can walk between the two.

blocks.html: Most people come to Lamphun to pay respects at Wat Phra That Hariphunchai and then leave, even though the museum that holds the town's full story is just a few steps across Inthayongyot Road. It isn't a big place. A real walk-through takes about 45 minutes to an hour. But what's on display are genuine pieces unearthed in Lamphun itself, which makes it clear that this town was the center of the Hariphunchai kingdom long before Chiang Mai even existed.

blocks.text: Why this museum is worth a stop

blocks.html: The collection began when the last ruler of Lamphun started gathering the town's antiquities around 1910. The Fine Arts Department then raised it to national-museum status in 1927, the current permanent building was finished in 1974, and Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn officially opened it in 1979. What sets it apart from the usual museum is that nearly everything is genuinely local, found in temples and archaeological sites around Lamphun rather than borrowed for display.

items: See three eras of art in one go — pre-Hariphunchai, Hariphunchai, and Lanna, laid out in sequence in one place.
Right next to Wat Phra That Hariphunchai — directly across from the temple, so you can pair the two on one trip without driving.
Not crowded — easy to wander, easy to photograph, no jostling for angles like at the famous temples.
Cheap entry — just a few baht for Thai visitors, and the knowledge you get is well worth it.

items.name: Phra Rod amulet
items.blurb: One of the Benjaphakhi set of amulets that collectors across the country chase, with its origin at Wat Mahawan in Lamphun. The piece on display belongs to the Fine Arts Department, so you can see the genuine mold and terracotta up close. This is the one amulet enthusiasts come specifically to see.

items.name: Ancient Mon inscriptions
items.blurb: The inscription room holds Hariphunchai-period stone slabs written in ancient Mon script, dating to roughly the 12th century, alongside later Lanna Tham-script inscriptions. They're primary evidence that this town used Mon before the northern Thai language.

items.name: Hariphunchai-period Buddha images
items.blurb: Hariphunchai-style Buddha images and heads with a distinctive face and large hair curls, different from the later Lanna style. Seen side by side, it's easy to spot how the forms changed over time.

items.name: Dvaravati art before Hariphunchai
items.blurb: Pre-Hariphunchai pieces that reflect Dvaravati influence from central Thailand, showing how that culture flowed north along the rivers before Lamphun became a town.

items.name: Ancient ceramics and everyday objects
items.blurb: Ceramics, earthenware vessels, and household items excavated from the Ban Wang Hai archaeological site, which help you picture what daily life was like for people in the old town.

items.name: Lanna-period sculpture
items.blurb: Lanna-era Buddha images and carvings displayed along the long gallery, closing out the town's story as Hariphunchai becomes part of Lanna.

blocks.title: Viewing tips
blocks.html: Start with the inscription room, then move to the long gallery where pieces are arranged by era, and the town's story reads in order without confusion. The label text is in both Thai and English, but the print is small, so bring your glasses if your eyesight isn't great.

The building isn't large, and the displays are arranged by era so you can walk through easily. It breaks down roughly into the zones below. Follow them in order and the town's story comes through most clearly.

items.name: Inscription room
items.blurb: Brings together Hariphunchai-period Mon-script stone inscriptions and Lanna Tham script. It's the heart of the museum, telling the town's language and religion.

items.name: Long gallery
items.blurb: Displays prehistoric tools from Ban Wang Hai, followed by Hariphunchai and Lanna Buddhist art arranged by era.

items.name: Special exhibition room
items.blurb: Rotating standout pieces and focused themes, such as Lamphun votive tablets and lesser-known works.

blocks.text: Hours, entry fees, and getting there

items: Hours — Wednesday to Sunday, 9:00 AM to 4:00 PM. Closed Mondays, Tuesdays, and public holidays.
Entry fee — around 20–30 THB for Thai visitors, 100–200 THB for foreigners (students in uniform and monks/novices enter free).
Location — Inthayongyot Road, across from Wat Phra That Hariphunchai, in the heart of Lamphun's old town.
Getting there — about a 30–40 minute drive from Chiang Mai, or take a songthaew/train into Lamphun town and then a tuk-tuk.
Time needed — an easy 45 minutes to 1 hour for a full look.

blocks.title: Check before you go
blocks.html: The hours and fees at Fine Arts Department museums are fairly stable, but before a long trip it's worth calling 053-511186 or checking the museum's Facebook page again, in case it's closed for repairs or hosting a special event.
The good thing about this place is that it's in the old-town area, all within walking distance. Plan a half day and you get the temple, the museum, and local food in a single trip.

items: Wat Phra That Hariphunchai — directly across the road; just walk over to pay respects at the town's guardian stupa.
Queen Chamadevi Monument — the first ruler who founded the town, not far from the town center.
Lamphun markets and restaurants — you can hunt down khanom jeen nam ngiao and other local dishes around the temple.

faq.q: What days is Hariphunchai National Museum open?
faq.a: It's open Wednesday to Sunday, 9:00 AM to 4:00 PM, and closed Mondays, Tuesdays, and public holidays. If you're planning an early-week visit, avoid those days or call ahead at 053-511186.

faq.q: How much is the entry fee?
faq.a: About 20–30 THB for Thai visitors and 100–200 THB for foreigners. Students in uniform and monks/novices enter free. It's a great value for what you get to see.

faq.q: What's the single best thing in the museum?
faq.a: The Phra Rod amulet, a Benjaphakhi-set amulet that originates at Wat Mahawan, is the piece people come specifically to see. After that, the ancient Mon inscriptions and Hariphunchai-period Buddha images, which are hard to find elsewhere.

faq.q: Does it take long to walk through?
faq.a: The building isn't large, so a thorough walk-through is about 45 minutes to an hour. It's a good stop before or after visiting Wat Phra That Hariphunchai across the road, and a half day covers both.

faq.q: Is it easy to get here from Chiang Mai?
faq.a: Yes. It's about a 30–40 minute drive from Chiang Mai to Lamphun town, or you can take the train or a songthaew into town and then a tuk-tuk. The museum is right in the old town, directly across from the temple.
